title: Custom RFID Card Printing — Full-Color Branding
summary: Proud Tek prints custom RFID and NFC cards in-house on the same Shenzhen lines that laminate and encode them — CMYK offset for volume runs, UV digital for short runs and white ink, screen printing for metallic and opaque effects, thermal transfer for variable data, and laser engraving for metal and premium cards. Every card is built to the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 format (85.6 × 54 mm, 0.76 mm), printed at 300 DPI with CMYK-plus-Pantone colour matching, then finished, personalised and chip-encoded to your data. This page is the print-and-finish reference: the process menu, the artwork-file specs prepress checks on every job, the proofing and colour-matching loop, and the QC records a procurement team can verify before a five-figure run goes to press. For chip data and programming detail, see the card encoding service.

sections.title: What custom RFID card printing actually covers
sections.intro: 'Custom card printing' can mean a logo dropped onto a stock white card, or a credential engineered from the artwork in. Proud Tek means the second: five print processes run in-house on the same lines that laminate and [encode](/lp/rfid-card-encoding-service/) the card, so the print, the finish and the chip data are one job with one owner — not three vendors pointing at each other. Match the process to your run size and the effect you need; the [card material guide](/blog/rfid-card-materials-pvc-pet-abs-wood/) covers the bodies those processes print on. The numbers below are the ones a print buyer checks first.
bullets: CMYK offset — photo-quality full colour at 300 DPI once the plates are made, the most consistent choice for volume runs and the reason it owns orders from 500 pcs up.
UV digital — no plate-making, so it owns short runs from 100 pcs, prototypes and rush work, and prints opaque white ink on transparent and dark card bodies.
Screen printing and hot stamping — opaque white, metallic and foil effects that four-colour process cannot reproduce, pressed into the card surface.
Thermal transfer — per-card names, photos, sequential numbers, barcodes and QR codes for badges, student IDs and membership programs, run as their own pass over the base artwork.
Laser engraving — permanent marking and serialisation for metal and wooden cards, the one process that cannot wear, fade or be lifted off.
Security printing — micro-text, guilloche, UV-fluorescent ink and holographic overlay lamination for tamper-resistant government, corporate and financial cards.

sections.title: The print-and-finish capability menu
sections.intro: This table is the fast way to see how your card gets built — body, print method, finish, personalisation and the chip encoding that rides along. Every card leaves on the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 footprint (85.6 × 54 mm), so it drops into any standard reader, wallet or issuance printer; the body and process decide the look and the run economics. Strong starting points are the [printed loyalty card](/products/rfid-cards/rfid-loyalty-card/) and the [metal business card](/products/rfid-cards/rfid-metal-business-card/); the [transparent NFC card](/products/rfid-cards/transparent-nfc-card/) shows what UV white ink does on a clear body.

image.alt: Cross-section anatomy of a printed RFID card beside a finish menu. The card is a five-layer stack: a protective overlay on top, a CMYK-printed PVC face, an inlay layer carrying the antenna coil and RFID chip, a printed PVC back, and a protective overlay beneath — laminated to the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 size, 85.6 by 54 mm at 0.76 mm thick with a 3.18 mm corner radius. To the right, a finish menu lists spot UV, hot foil, matte or gloss lamination, magnetic stripe, signature panel and custom die-cut, each applied as a separate pass after lamination.

rows: Gloss or matte lamination, spot UV
Name / photo / serial + chip encoded & read-verified

bullets: Finishing is a separate production pass, so effects add cost individually — pick the one or two that carry the design rather than stacking all of them. Spot UV, hot foil (gold, silver, rose gold or holographic), embossed numbering, signature panels and custom die-cut shapes are applied in-house after lamination and before final QC.

Magnetic stripe lamination — HiCo or LoCo — and a contact smart-card module (ISO 7816) can be added for hotel-lock, transit and dual-interface cards that need both contactless and legacy compatibility.

Print on any card chip we stock and allocate directly from NXP, Impinj and EM — MIFARE Classic and DESFire, NTAG 213/215/216, NTAG 424 DNA, EM4200 or UHF UCODE 9 — each encoded and 100% read-verified to ISO/IEC 14443 before it ships (data detail on the [encoding service](/lp/rfid-card-encoding-service/)).

sections.title: Artwork files that print right the first time
sections.intro: Most print delays are artwork delays, and nearly all of them are fixable at file handoff instead of on the proof. Prepress checks every incoming file against the specs below and flags anything that fails with a free correction pass — a web-resolution logo caught on day one costs nothing; the same logo caught on a printed proof costs a week. Send only brand guidelines and a logo and the design team builds the print-ready layout, chip and antenna zones included, at no charge.

callout.text: Send brand guidelines and a logo and our design team prepares the print-ready card layout — bleed, safe zone, chip and antenna zones and colour setup — at no charge, then a digital proof for your sign-off before anything goes to press.

sections.title: Proofing, colour matching and production
sections.intro: Nothing prints at volume until you approve a proof. A digital proof settles layout, copy and colour intent on every order; for Pantone-critical brand work the press is calibrated to your references and a printed proof goes out before the run commits. The loop costs a few days and removes the most expensive failure mode in card printing — a five-figure run in the wrong colour. Offset colour is held to ISO 12647-2 process control, so brand blue means the same thing on reorder four as it did on the first press check; when the printed serial must also match the chip, print-and-encode is one workflow on the [encoding line](/lp/rfid-card-encoding-service/).

image.alt: A five-step print-and-encode production flow, left to right. Step 1, artwork and file check: format, resolution, bleed and colour verified or corrected. Step 2, digital proof approved before any plate is cut. Step 3, print — CMYK offset or UV digital at 300 DPI — then laminate and die-cut to the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 size. Step 4, finish and personalise: spot UV, hot foil, magnetic stripe, plus per-card serials, photos and barcodes. Step 5, encode the chip and 100% read-verify, matching printed serial to encoded data, then pack with the document set. A base arrow reads from brand guidelines to a finished, encoded card.

faq.question: What file format and setup do you need for RFID card artwork?
faq.answer: Vector Adobe Illustrator (.ai) or a print-ready PDF is preferred; high-resolution PSD, CDR and PNG/JPEG are accepted. Supply art at 300 DPI minimum at final card size, with 3 mm bleed on all sides, CMYK colour mode (Pantone spot references called out separately) and all text converted to outlines. Prepress checks every file for free and, if you only have a logo and brand guidelines, builds the print-ready layout — chip and antenna zones included — at no additional cost.

faq.question: How do you match our brand's Pantone colours?
faq.answer: For offset printing we use Pantone spot inks for exact brand colour, and hold the run to ISO 12647-2 offset process control so the colour is repeatable on every reorder. For UV digital printing we calibrate the press to your Pantone references and send a printed colour proof for approval before the full run begins. Either way, colour is signed off on a proof before volume commits.

faq.question: Can you print and serialise different data on each card in a batch?
faq.answer: Yes. Thermal transfer and variable-data inkjet print unique names, photos, sequential numbers, barcodes and QR codes per card within one production batch, and laser engraving marks permanent serials on metal and wooden cards. Supply a CSV or Excel file and each card prints against its row. When the printed serial must also match the chip's encoded data, that print-to-chip matching runs as one workflow on the encoding line and is 100% read-verified.

faq.question: What size and thickness are the cards, and will they fit standard readers?
faq.answer: Standard cards are built to the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 (CR-80) format — 85.6 × 54 mm at 0.76 mm thick with a ~3.18 mm corner radius — the same footprint as a bank or access card, so they feed through issuance printers and read on standard 13.56 MHz and UHF readers and hotel locks. Mini cards, key tags and custom die-cut shapes are available where a non-standard form factor is the point.

faq.question: How long does custom card printing take, and can I see a sample first?
faq.answer: Printed runs typically complete within 7-12 working days after proof approval, depending on process and finishing — UV digital short runs sit at the faster end; offset runs with multiple finishing passes take longer. International express shipping then adds 3-5 days to North America and Europe. Free samples of standard products (typically 3-5 pieces) ship first, and a custom printed proof of your own artwork carries a small setup fee credited against the production order.
